notes.meaning: Jericho was locked up tight because the people inside were terrified of the Israelites. The city gates were barred shut, so nobody could leave or enter. God noted how secure the fortress seemed to show that human defenses could not stop His plans.

The Lord spoke to Joshua and declared that He had already handed Jericho, its king, and its warriors over to Israel. Even though the battle had not started yet, God spoke of the victory as something already finished. God's people can trust His promises before they see the final result.

God gave Joshua an unusual battle plan instead of normal siege warfare. The army and seven priests carrying ram's-horn trumpets were to march once around the city each day for six days, guarding the ark of the covenant. On the seventh day, they would circle seven times, blow a long trumpet blast, and shout so the city walls would collapse to the ground.

Joshua gathered the priests and soldiers to pass along God's exact commands. He ordered the priests to carry the sacred ark with seven priests blowing horns ahead of it, while armed troops led the way. Joshua showed quick and complete obedience by following God's unusual orders without delay.

The march began in the exact order God commanded. Armed troops walked in front, followed by seven priests blowing their horns, then the ark of the Lord, and finally the rear guard. Putting the ark near the center showed that God Himself was leading the procession and fighting the battle.

Joshua commanded the soldiers to march in total silence until he gave the signal to shout. They walked around Jericho once without saying a single word, listening only to the horns, and then returned to camp to sleep. This silence tested their patience and kept the defenders of Jericho in fearful suspense.

Joshua got up early the next morning, and the priests and soldiers repeated the march around the city. They did this once every day for six days, returning to their camp at Gilgal each afternoon. This daily routine taught the people to wait patiently on God's timing instead of rushing into battle.

On the seventh day, the army woke up at dawn to circle the city seven times. This was the only day they marched around more than once. The repeated circuits marked the special completion of God's work of judgment.

At the end of the seventh lap, when the priests blew their horns, Joshua ordered the people to shout. He told them to shout because the Lord had officially given them the city. Their shout expressed bold faith and joy in God's victory before the walls had even moved.

Joshua declared that the city and everything inside it was devoted to the Lord for total destruction. Only Rahab and the relatives inside her home were spared because she had protected Israel's spies. As the first conquered city in Canaan, Jericho belonged entirely to God as a first gift.

Joshua strictly warned the soldiers not to steal anything set apart for destruction, because taking those things would bring a curse upon the whole camp. All articles of silver, gold, bronze, and iron were declared holy to the Lord and had to go into His sanctuary treasury. This command kept Israel from fighting for selfish gain and reminded them that the spoils belonged to God.

When the horns blew a long blast, the people raised a massive shout, and the walls of Jericho fell flat to the ground. The soldiers charged straight ahead from every direction and captured the city. God performed this miracle to show that His power, not human weapons, brought down the fortress.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars argue that the walls fell through natural causes, such as an earthquake or military undermining, rather than a direct miracle.

notes.meaning: The Israelites destroyed everything in the city with their swords, including men, women, children, and livestock. God commanded this complete judgment because the Canaanites had lived in deep idolatry and evil for centuries. The army acted as God's ministers of justice rather than fighting for personal plunder.

Joshua instructed the two spies to enter Rahab's house and rescue her family, keeping the solemn promise they had made. The spies brought out Rahab, her parents, her siblings, and all who belonged to her, placing them safely outside Israel's camp. They stayed outside the camp for a time to turn away from pagan customs before joining God's people.

The Israelites burned Jericho and everything within it to the ground. They kept only the metals, placing the silver, gold, bronze, and iron into the treasury of the Lord's tabernacle. Dedicating these metals honored God by giving the very first wealth of the land to His house.

Joshua kept Rahab and her family alive, and her family continued living among the Israelites. God welcomed her because she turned to Him in faith and protected His messengers, even making her an ancestor of King David and Jesus. Her rescue shows that God extends mercy to anyone who puts their trust in Him.

Joshua announced a solemn curse on anyone who would ever try to rebuild the fortress of Jericho. He warned that the builder would lose his oldest son when laying the foundation and his youngest son when setting up the gates. God wanted the ruins to remain as a lasting sign of His justice against evil.

The Lord stayed with Joshua, guiding him and giving him success in every battle. News of Joshua's leadership and the fall of Jericho spread quickly throughout the entire region. When God is with a leader, His presence brings true honor and fulfills His promises.
